messages.author: 343fd12501b7fca4
messages.subject: Interpolation between locations?
parts:
Hi Chris,

Pardon this very basic question - but does AKDE interpolate use between locations in the sense that BBMM or BRB does?

I understand the estimator incorporates time between points, but I also see that it functions as a KDE would when samples are separated by enough time that autocorrelation reduces greatly.

The reason that I ask is that I have GPS data for a very mobile species (bobcats) that has variable intervals due to very low fix success. Some points are separated by as little as 1 hour, while other points are separated by several days. As a result, the steps with very long time lags need to be discarded from these aforementioned movement modeling approaches to avoid overestimation. The problem is that these data with long time lags make up a large chunk of the data for some individuals, and I am losing a lot of information by discarding them. So, I have chunks of highly correlated points interspersed with less correlated points.

My current understanding is that I may need to either discard the less autocorrelated data to fit a movement model, or downgrade to an estimator that assumes independence such as standard KDE or LoCoH. I would greatly appreciate any insight you have on this.

Thanks much,
Dave

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Interpolation between locations?
parts:
Hi Dave,

Sampling irregularity can be accounted for in AKDE by optimally weighting the data (the weights option in akde()):
  • https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eap.1704
  • https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/bandwidth.html

When I first derived AKDE, I also derived a separate estimator that filled in the gaps (a hybrid between AKDE and the Kriged occurrence distribution), so it is possible. However, when gaps are short, then the optimal bandwidth is much larger than the gaps, making this fruitless. On the other hand, when there are large gaps, then by filling them in you get a over-smoothed estimate and give up asymptotic consistency. Optimal weights fixes the same problem in a much better way.

Best,
Chris
